title: Mixture of Experts and Parallelism: Capacity, Routing, and Communication
summary: Understand why sparse activation saves arithmetic without eliminating memory or communication, and choose parallelism around the actual bottleneck.
learningObjectives: Distinguish total parameters, active parameters, and actual runtime cost.
Calculate expert capacity, routing imbalance, and activation traffic.
Explain data, tensor, pipeline, and expert parallelism.
Defend a topology-aware design with explicit failure and quality budgets.

sections.title: 1. Separate model capacity from work per token
paragraphs: Large language models (LLMs) like ChatGPT or Claude are built from a stack of transformer layers, and each layer has two main parts: attention, which mixes information between tokens, and a feed-forward network (FFN), a small neural network applied to each token on its own. (Both are covered in the Inside a decoder: from text to the next token article.) This article covers two ideas that come up once these models get very large: mixture of experts, a way to grow a model without growing the work done per token, and parallelism, the ways a model gets split across many GPUs. First, let's pin down what "big" means for a model. A dense transformer normally applies the same feed-forward network to every token at a given layer. A mixture-of-experts (MoE) layer supplies several feed-forward networks, called experts, plus a small learned component called a router that selects a small subset for each token. Each expert is a learned function, usually a multilayer perceptron (MLP, the same kind of feed-forward network a dense layer uses), rather than a separate chatbot or a manually assigned subject specialist. Attention and other shared components still run for every token. Conditional execution changes which weights participate; it does not make those weights disappear from storage.

Because of that, it helps to track three separate ledgers: total parameters determine weight storage, active parameters approximate selected matrix work per token, and execution cost includes communication, memory movement, attention, and scheduling. So parameter count alone isn't enough to compare latency. The experts selected across an entire batch can cover the whole model even when each individual token selects very few. Serving memory must accommodate the deployed weights or explicitly pay for moving them between storage tiers. A rough analogy is a restaurant kitchen with sixteen cooking stations where each order only visits two of them: each order takes about as much cooking as it would in a small kitchen, but you still pay rent on floor space for all sixteen stations, and staff still have to carry orders between them.

To make this concrete, consider an invented architecture with 2 billion shared parameters and 16 expert groups containing 0.5 billion parameters each, where each group represents the expert weights accumulated across the model's MoE layers. With top-2 selection at each layer (each token goes to its two highest-scoring experts; the next section shows how that choice is made), total parameters are 10 billion and the per-token active equivalent is 3 billion. At two bytes per weight, weights occupy 20 GB in decimal units before runtime buffers, caches (such as the KV cache covered in the Serving LLMs: KV Cache as a Memory and Latency Budget article), gradients, or optimizer state. A 3-billion-parameter dense model needs 6 GB of weights under the same assumption. The formula box below writes this accounting in general form, and the figure at the end of this section compares the numbers side by side. These are capacity calculations, not claims of equal quality or throughput.
sections.formula: P_total = P_shared + E × P_expert; P_active ≈ P_shared + k × P_expert

sections.title: 2. Follow the token through routing
paragraphs: With the accounting in place, let's follow one token through an MoE layer. By the time a token reaches this layer, it is represented as a hidden state: a vector of numbers that earlier layers have been refining. A typical router projects that token representation into one score per expert. A softmax turns the scores into probabilities, and a top-k operation keeps the k highest-scoring experts as destinations. The probabilities of the chosen experts become gate weights, which say how much each expert's output counts. The implementation then groups token activations by destination (dispatch), executes the expert matrices, restores token order and combines the returned outputs with the gate weights (combine). Gate normalization conventions vary, so an implementation must state whether selected probabilities are renormalized. The hard destination choice is discrete, while selected gate values provide a differentiable path for training. The animation below walks through a toy top-1 case with three tokens and two experts: A and C go to expert 1, B goes to expert 0, and the outputs are put back in A, B, C order afterward.

One problem you might run into is a router that learns to favor a few experts, overloading them while others sit mostly idle. Switch Transformers, an MoE model from Google, uses top-1 routing (each token goes to exactly one expert) and adds an auxiliary balancing term, an extra loss that nudges the router toward spreading tokens out. That term is based on the fraction of tokens assigned to each expert and the average router probability for that expert. For T tokens and E experts, let f_i be the hard top-1 assignment fraction and p̄_i the mean soft probability. The formula at the end of this section (where α is a small weighting coefficient) encourages the router to avoid concentrating work. It is an optimization pressure, not a guarantee of uniform assignments in each batch. The hard counts are usually treated as nondifferentiable in this term. [Switch Transformers](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/volume23/21-0998/21-0998.pdf)

In practice, inspect assignments before and after capacity filtering (experts usually have a fixed number of token slots, which the next section covers). A low reported loss can conceal dropped traffic if metrics count only accepted tokens. Monitor expert token counts, maximum-to-mean load, router entropy (a measure of how spread out the router's probabilities are), and overflow alongside task quality. Entropy alone is insufficient: soft probabilities may look broad while deterministic tie-breaking repeatedly chooses the same expert. Routing decisions depend on contextual representations, so a token spelling does not have one permanent expert destination. The figure at the end of this section summarizes the whole path from scoring to combining, and notes that dispatch and combine become network traffic once experts live on different devices.
sections.formula: L_balance = α × E × Σ_i(f_i × p̄_i); Σ_i f_i = Σ_i p̄_i = 1 for top-1 routing

sections.title: 3. Imbalance turns capacity into a quality decision
paragraphs: Routing decides where each token wants to go, but each expert can only take so many. A fixed-capacity implementation reserves C token slots per expert for a routing group (the set of tokens routed together, such as one batch). Think of each expert as a checkout lane with a fixed number of spots in line: if lots of shoppers pick the same lane, some won't fit even while other lanes sit empty. Under an explicit top-k assignment convention, a useful planning formula is C = ceil(c × T × k / E), where c is the capacity factor, a multiplier above 1 that adds headroom beyond a perfectly even split. Libraries may define capacity differently, so verify the actual implementation. GShard, an early large-scale MoE system from Google, uses bounded expert capacity and handling for overflow; the general lesson is that routing and memory allocation cannot be designed independently. [GShard](https://arxiv.org/html/2006.16668v1)

For an invented group of 4,096 tokens, 16 experts, top-2 routing, and capacity factor 1.25, mean load is 512 assignments and each expert has 640 slots. If one expert receives 900 assignments, 260 exceed its local capacity even if other experts have free slots. Reserved capacity totals 10,240 assignments versus 8,192 requested assignments, a 25% padding allowance. Global free space does not resolve a local destination bottleneck without rerouting or changing allocation. The figure at the end of this section shows these numbers: mean demand, per-expert capacity, the hot expert's demand, and the resulting overflow.

So what happens to the overflow? Token dropping generally means skipping an overflowing expert contribution, not deleting the token from the sequence; the residual path (the skip connection that adds each sublayer's output back onto its input, covered in the Inside a decoder article) can still carry its representation. This affects the computation the model receives and must be evaluated for quality, especially under domain shifts. Increasing capacity consumes memory and possibly padded compute. Dropless execution, which finds room for every assignment, avoids that particular quality tradeoff but still faces skewed expert runtimes and finite memory. MegaBlocks shows how block-sparse kernels (GPU routines that multiply matrices built from variable-sized blocks) can handle variable expert workloads without dropping tokens. This is an implementation capability, not a promise that arbitrary traffic fits. [MegaBlocks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.15841)
sections.formula: C = ceil(cTk/E); example: ceil(1.25 × 4096 × 2 / 16) = 640 slots per expert

sections.title: 4. Four parallelism dimensions solve different problems
paragraphs: So far we've looked at one MoE layer on its own. Real models are often too large, or too slow to train, on a single GPU, so the work gets spread across many devices. There are four common ways to split it, and each one solves a different problem. First up is data parallelism, which replicates a logical model across workers processing different examples, then aggregates corresponding gradients during training. It increases aggregate training throughput but does not, by itself, reduce the weight memory of one replica. Sharded optimizer or parameter approaches (such as ZeRO or FSDP, which split those replicated copies across workers) add a separate memory strategy. In inference, independent replicas serve different requests without gradient synchronization.

Next, tensor parallelism partitions individual matrix operations across devices. Partial results require collectives (communication operations where a group of devices exchange or combine data together, such as an all-reduce that sums values across devices), often inside every transformer block, making communication frequency important. Pipeline parallelism instead partitions consecutive layers into stages, a bit like an assembly line where each station owns a few layers. Activations cross stage boundaries, and microbatches (small slices of a batch fed in one after another) keep stages busy. Too few microbatches leave startup and drain bubbles (idle time while the line fills up and empties out); unequal stage times create persistent idle time. Megatron's work (from NVIDIA's large-model training project) explains how tensor, pipeline, and data parallelism can be composed. [Megatron-LM parallelism study](https://arxiv.org/html/2104.04473v5) The walkthrough below shows these first three dimensions on two devices with tiny 2×2 weights: copied weights for data parallelism, one matrix split by rows for tensor parallelism, and consecutive layers for pipeline parallelism.

The fourth dimension, expert parallelism, places different experts on different devices and moves token representations to the weights. That is the dispatch and return you saw in the routing animation in section 2. It is distinct from tensor parallelism: an expert may fit entirely on one device, or its matrices may themselves be sharded. Every axis needs an explicit process group (the set of ranks that communicate for that axis, where a rank is one worker process, usually one GPU) and ownership rule. Multiplying four configuration integers blindly can double-count workers because some frameworks arrange expert parallel groups within a broader data-parallel dimension. Draw the actual ranks, identify where each parameter is replicated, and specify which ranks synchronize its gradients. The figure at the end of this section compares what each of the four dimensions distributes.

sections.title: 5. Calculate traffic before predicting speed
paragraphs: Once experts live on different devices, every MoE layer has to ship tokens across the network and back, so it's worth estimating that traffic before guessing at speed. Suppose an expert-parallel group handles T = 8,192 token representations in one MoE layer, hidden width d = 4,096 (numbers per token vector), top-2 routing (k = 2), and two-byte activations (b = 2). Dispatch payload is T × k × d × b = 134,217,728 bytes, or 128 MiB. Returning equally sized expert outputs doubles the logical payload to 256 MiB. This is group-wide payload before accounting for local destinations, protocol overhead, padding, or backward communication; it is not the traffic injected by each device.

Next, let's turn that group-wide number into a per-device one. With eight uniformly loaded devices, each originates one eighth of that traffic, or 32 MiB across dispatch and return. If destinations are independently uniform, seven eighths travels remotely: approximately 28 MiB sent per device. At an assumed effective injection bandwidth of 25 GB/s, this is about 1.17 milliseconds of serialization per device. Receive traffic, collective phases, network contention, and dependencies determine elapsed time; this calculation is only a lower-bound planning component under the stated assumptions.

Bytes are only part of the picture, though. A simple communication model separates startup latency α (a fixed cost paid for every message, however small) from size divided by effective bandwidth B. Shipping packages is a decent analogy: each shipment has fixed paperwork plus a cost that grows with weight, so a thousand tiny packages can cost more than one big crate. Large prefill batches (processing a whole prompt at once) can become bandwidth constrained; small decode batches (generating one new token at a time per request) may spend more time initiating many short exchanges than transferring bytes. Doubling bandwidth cannot remove launch and synchronization latency. Conversely, reducing expert batch sizes to minimize waiting can produce inefficient tiny matrix multiplies. Measure tokens per expert and message sizes at the actual concurrency distribution before attributing poor utilization to insufficient GPU arithmetic. Prefill and decode are covered in more depth in the Serving LLMs: KV Cache as a Memory and Latency Budget article, and the figure at the end of this section plots this simple model, showing startup latency dominating small payloads.
sections.formula: Logical forward payload ≈ 2Tkdb bytes; communication time ≈ n_messages × α + transferred_bytes / B_effective

sections.title: 6. Place communication on the right links
paragraphs: Knowing how much traffic there is leads to the next question: which physical links it travels over. Topology describes which devices share fast links, host interfaces, switches, and failure domains (groups of hardware that tend to fail together, like the GPUs in one server). Aggregate advertised network bandwidth is not necessarily available between every pair of ranks simultaneously. A topology-aware mapping should keep frequent tensor collectives within a fast local group where possible and evaluate expert all-to-all traffic (every device sending some tokens to every other device) against the inter-node fabric's bisection bandwidth (roughly, the bandwidth available when one half of the cluster talks to the other half). This placement rule is an engineering heuristic, not a universal optimum: large expert weights may force broader distribution.

Pipeline boundaries may be a better place to cross slower links when their traffic is less frequent, but sequence length, microbatch count, and scheduling can reverse that conclusion. The original Megatron tensor-parallel design reduces synchronization by choosing complementary matrix partitions within transformer sublayers. This illustrates why placement and operation layout should be reasoned about together. [Megatron tensor parallelism](https://research.nvidia.com/labs/adlr/MegatronLM/)

Putting this together, build a rank map (a record of which rank owns which layers, tensor slices and experts, and where it sits physically) before implementation. For each collective, record participants, bytes, frequency, and the slowest shared resource. Then inspect overlap: independent computation can hide some transfer, but a token cannot consume an expert result before it returns. An apparently balanced rank map can still overload one network interface if several devices share it. Tests should include realistic mixed sequence lengths and bursty expert choices; uniform synthetic tokens can hide both routing hotspots and communication contention. The figure at the end of this section lays out this process as a sequence of steps.

sections.title: 7. Capacity and failure are model-level properties
paragraphs: Spreading a model across many devices also changes what a hardware failure means. A single expert shard may be necessary for the model's next token, so losing one device can make an entire distributed replica unavailable. Removing the unavailable expert from the router silently changes model behavior. Treat such fallback as a separately evaluated policy. A safer operational baseline is to stop admission (accepting new requests) to the unhealthy replica, retry eligible requests on a complete healthy replica, and restore the missing state before rejoining service.

Budget memory for all resident weights, KV cache (the per-request attention state covered in the Serving LLMs article), temporary dispatch buffers, expert activations, and communication workspaces. Training additionally needs gradients, optimizer states, saved activations, and checkpoint staging according to the chosen sharding scheme. A model that barely fits average traffic can fail when a hot expert receives a burst or longer requests expand the cache. Spare capacity is therefore a concrete concurrency and recovery budget, not just unused hardware.

Expert replication can reduce hotspots, but adds memory consumption and routing complexity; during training replicas also need consistent weight updates. Checkpoint metadata must preserve parameter identities and shard layouts so recovery can reconstruct the intended model. Define admission limits from measured worst-case buffers, then test device loss and workload skew independently. Otherwise a recovery plan may only work when the remaining cluster has unusually low demand.

sections.title: 8. Defend the design with a bottleneck hypothesis
paragraphs: To wrap up, let's put the pieces together for an interview. Begin with the workload and service objective: training versus inference, prompt lengths, generation lengths, concurrency, quality tolerance, and available interconnect. State the memory floor from total weights and runtime state. Estimate selected expert work and activation traffic separately. Choose a parallelism layout, then explain which measurement would falsify the choice. This makes the answer testable instead of presenting parallelism as a menu of fashionable techniques.

Compare candidate layouts at equal quality and comparable hardware budgets. Track end-to-end throughput, time to first token, inter-token latency (both covered in the Serving LLMs article), maximum expert load, overflow rate, and communication time. A faster kernel is not sufficient if synchronization dominates or dropping damages important workloads. The winning architecture is the one whose quality, capacity, network behavior, and recovery plan remain acceptable under the workload you actually intend to support.

interview.question: A 10-billion-total, 3-billion-active MoE model is slower than a 3-billion dense model during low-concurrency decoding on eight GPUs. How would you investigate and redesign it?
interview.answer: First verify comparable quality, precision, and request lengths. The MoE still stores 20 GB of two-byte weights and may invoke multiple short dispatch and combine exchanges per layer. Profile per-expert token counts, kernel occupancy, collective startup, and link contention. Low-concurrency decoding may be latency dominated even when payload volume is small. Try fewer expert-parallel ranks if memory permits, placement within a faster link domain, or additional independent replicas to avoid unnecessarily broad collectives. Increase batching only within the latency budget. Preserve routing semantics and validate quality if capacity or fallback policy changes. Benchmark the full service and test a failed rank before committing.
followUps: What changes when prompt prefill becomes the dominant workload?
How would you distinguish a hot expert from a congested network interface?
When would expert replication help, and what additional state must training synchronize?

pitfalls: Treating active parameter count as the memory requirement or a latency prediction.
Assuming balancing loss guarantees per-batch load equality.
Counting group-wide payload as per-device bytes, or equating injection bandwidth with end-to-end collective bandwidth.
Assuming spare capacity on one expert automatically absorbs another expert's overflow.
Silently changing routing after shard failure without validating quality.
Multiplying parallelism degrees without verifying process-group overlap.
checklist: Write total and active parameter accounting with precision and excluded overheads.
Specify router top-k, gate normalization, capacity convention, and overflow behavior.
Map actual ranks and parameter ownership for every parallelism dimension.
Estimate per-device remote bytes and distinguish startup latency from bandwidth.
Measure expert skew, quality, end-to-end latency, and memory under representative traffic.
Reserve recovery headroom and test loss of an expert-owning device.

flashcards.front: Why do total and active parameters answer different questions?
flashcards.back: Total parameters govern stored model capacity; active parameters estimate selected weight operations for one token. Communication, attention, and memory movement still affect execution.

flashcards.front: Is an MoE expert necessarily a specialist in a named topic?
flashcards.back: No. It is a learned subnetwork selected from contextual hidden states. Semantic specialization may emerge, but named domains are not guaranteed.

flashcards.front: With 2B shared weights, 16 experts of 0.5B each, and top-2 routing, what are total and active counts?
flashcards.back: Total is 2 + 16 × 0.5 = 10B; active equivalent is 2 + 2 × 0.5 = 3B, excluding small router overhead. Two-byte storage still requires 20 GB for all weights.

flashcards.front: What does the Switch balancing loss use?
flashcards.back: It combines hard assignment fractions with mean soft router probabilities, scaled by the expert count and a coefficient. It encourages spread but cannot guarantee equal load in every batch.

flashcards.front: Compute capacity for T=4096, k=2, E=16, and c=1.25.
flashcards.back: Under C=ceil(cTk/E), capacity is 640 assignments per expert. The mean is 512, but skew can overflow one expert despite spare slots elsewhere.

flashcards.front: Does token dropping delete a token from the sequence?
flashcards.back: Usually it skips an overflowing expert contribution while the residual representation continues. This changes model computation and requires quality evaluation.
No. It avoids skipping contributions, but hot experts can still create stragglers and memory pressure. Variable-size kernels address padding efficiency, not unlimited capacity.

flashcards.front: What does ordinary data parallelism distribute?
flashcards.back: Different examples across model replicas. Corresponding gradients synchronize during training; weight memory is not reduced unless an additional sharding strategy is used.

flashcards.front: Why does tensor parallelism prefer fast links?
flashcards.back: A layer's matrices are split across ranks and partial results communicate frequently. Repeated collective latency and bandwidth can dominate small workloads.
They allow different stages to work simultaneously. Too few microbatches cause fill and drain bubbles, while stage imbalance remains a separate bottleneck.

flashcards.front: How is expert parallelism different from tensor parallelism?
flashcards.back: Expert parallelism distributes distinct expert networks and routes tokens to them. Tensor parallelism splits an individual operation; an expert can also be tensor sharded.

flashcards.front: What is the logical forward activation payload for one MoE layer?
flashcards.back: Approximately 2Tkdb bytes for dispatch and return, assuming equal-sized outputs. It is group-wide and excludes local-route savings, metadata, padding, and backward traffic.

flashcards.front: Why might more bandwidth fail to accelerate low-concurrency decode?
flashcards.back: Tiny expert batches can be dominated by collective startup and kernel launch latency. Higher bandwidth reduces transfer time but not those fixed costs.

flashcards.front: Why is losing one expert-owning device potentially a replica-wide failure?
flashcards.back: The next token may require that shard. Removing it changes model behavior, so a complete healthy replica or an explicitly evaluated fallback is needed.
